tip: 갈아타요 (garatayo = transfer) splits into 갈아 (gara = change) + 타다 (tada = ride) – literally 'change-ride', which is exactly what a transfer is.
Transferring is 'change-riding': 갈아타요 (garatayo) = 갈다 (galda = change) + 타다 (tada = ride). Korean fuses the two verbs into one word.
Korean usually skips a 'have' verb – things just exist to you: 티머니 카드가 있어요 (timeoni kadeuga isseoyo) is literally 'a T-money card exists'. 있다 (itda) covers 'there is' and 'I have'.
Korean counts big numbers in ten-thousands: 만 원 (man won) = 10,000 won, and 만 (man) is its own unit – not built as ten × thousand the way English says it.
보다 (boda) after a noun means 'than': 버스보다 빨라요 (beoseuboda ppallayo = faster than the bus). The thing you compare against carries the marker, not the subject.
Korean says 'people are many', not 'there are many people': 사람이 정말 많아요 (sarami jeongmal manayo). The describing verb 많다 (manta) does all the work.
놓치다 (nochida = miss) is for things that get away – 막차를 놓쳤어요 (makchareul nochyeosseoyo). Missing a person uses a different verb, 보고 싶다 (bogo sipda).
'After' comes after: 10분 후에 (sipbun hue) is literally '10 minutes after-at'. 후 (hu) follows the time span instead of leading it like English 'in ten minutes'.
'There weren't any' is one verb: 자리가 없었어요 (jariga eopseosseoyo) = 'seats not-existed'. 없다 (eopda) packs 'not' and 'exist' together – no separate negative word.
Korean drops the 'one': 1,500 is 천오백 (cheonobaek), not 일천오백 (ilcheonobaek). 천 (cheon = thousand) and 백 (baek = hundred) stand alone when there is just one of them.
도 (do = too) stacks onto other particles: 버스에서도 (beoseueseodo) = 'on the bus too'. 에서 (eseo) stays put and 도 attaches right after it.
까지 (kkaji) covers both 'to' a place and 'until' a time: 공항까지 (gonghangkkaji = to the airport). One particle does the job of two English words.
There is no word 'traffic' here – the road itself is blocked: 길이 많이 막혀요 (giri mani makyeoyo) = 'the road is really clogged'. That is the everyday way to talk about traffic.
내릴게요 (naerilgeyo) uses the -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) ending to flag an action the listener should know about – you're telling the driver you're getting off, not predicting it.
Paying is 'calculating': 카드로 계산했어요 (kadeuro gyesanhaesseoyo) = 'I calculated by card'. 계산하다 (gyesanhada) covers both doing math and settling a bill.
보다 (boda = than) attaches to the thing you compare against: 택시보다 지하철이 싸요 (taeksiboda jihacheori ssayo) runs 'than taxis, the subway is cheap'.
달 (dal) means both moon and month – 다음 달 (daeum dal = next month) is literally 'next moon', a leftover from moon-based months.
에서 (eseo) and 까지 (kkaji) bracket a route as 'from...to': 서울에서 부산까지 (seoureseo busankkaji = from Seoul to Busan).
Clock time mixes both number systems: hours take native numbers – 두 시 (du si = two o'clock) – while minutes switch to Sino-Korean with 분 (bun).
You don't get lost in Korean – you lose the road: 길을 잃어버렸어요 (gireul ireobeoryeosseoyo) = 'I lost the way'. The road is the object, you stay the subject.
저기요 (jeogiyo) is literally 'over there!' – and it is a standard polite way to hail a stranger or a waiter, where English says 'excuse me'.
(으)로 (euro) marks direction: 오른쪽으로 (oreunjjogeuro = to the right).
사거리 (sageori = intersection) breaks into 사 (sa = four) + 거리 (geori = street): where four roads meet.
Position words come after the noun: 은행 앞에서 (eunhaeng apeseo) = 'bank front-at' = in front of the bank. 앞 (ap = front) is a noun that follows what it locates.
Subway exits are numbered: 4번 출구 (sabeon chulgu = exit 4) – a common way Koreans set meeting spots.
한테 (hante = to) marks the person you ask: 직원한테 물어봤어요 (jigwonhante mureobwasseoyo). Questions go 'to' someone – you ask to the staff, not ask the staff.
이제 (ije) is 'now' with a before/after edge – something changed: 이제 알아요 (ije arayo) = now I know, I didn't before. Plain 'right now' is 지금 (jigeum).
Sino-Korean numbers stack: 삼십 (samsip = thirty) = 삼 (sam = 3) × 십 (sip = 10).
보다 (boda = than) attaches to abstract nouns too: 생각보다 (saenggakboda) is literally 'than thought' – the everyday way to say 'than I expected'.
시간 (sigan = hours of duration) takes native numbers: 한 시간 (han sigan).
